utterances: Sanskrit: नासिका. sound: nāsikā. meaning: nose.
Sanskrit: मम नासिका. sound: mama nāsikā. meaning: my nose.

segments.text: Feminine, marked by the same -आ you will hear again.
ना is nā, न under the long-ā sign. सि is स under a short-i. का closes it, क under long-ā again: nā-si-kā.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — kin to two words, parent of neither

segments.text: नासिका (nāsikā) is built on an older word, नासा (nāsā), "nose," plus the diminutive suffix -इका. नासा itself, and the still-older root नस् (nas) behind it, go back to PIE nehas-, the unbroken root of English nose and Latin nasus ( becomes nasal).

Here is the correction worth making carefully: नासिका (nāsikā) is not the ancestor of Bengali nāk or Gujarati nāk. Both of those wore straight down from नस् itself, through Prakrit ṇakka, by adding a completely different suffix. नासिका (nāsikā) and नाक share a root, the way ग्रह् and English grab share one — relatives, not parent and child. Reaching for the nearest-looking Sanskrit word is not always reaching for the right ancestor.

segments.text: What PIE root is नासिका (nāsikā)'s family from, and name two of its Western cousins. (nehas-; nose, nasus/nasal.) Is नासिका (nāsikā) the ancestor of Bengali nāk, or its relative? (Relative — both descend from नस्, neither from the other.) What did you learn just before this? (Mukham, mouth.)

lessons.title: हृदयम् (hṛdayam) — "heart," a root barely disguised anywhere
lessons.gloss: heart — the oldest, most secure cousin this book has shown, and kept whole two chapters east

You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say "nose," "eye," and "mouth." (Nāsikā, akṣi, mukham.) One last word, and it names what this whole chapter has been checking on.

utterances: Sanskrit: हृदयम्. sound: hṛdayam. meaning: heart.
Sanskrit: मम हृदयम्. sound: mama hṛdayam. meaning: my heart.

segments.text: Neuter — the family this whole chapter keeps returning to.
हृ is hṛ: ह ha carrying the vocalic ऋ, the same buzzing vowel you first sounded out in गृह्णाति. द is da, य is ya, म् closes it neuter: hṛ-da-ya-m.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a root barely disguised anywhere

segments.text: हृदयम् (hṛdayam) is PIE kerd-, and almost nothing about it has changed shape on the way anywhere: English heart, Latin cor, genitive cordis ( becomes cordial, courage, accord), Greek kardia ( becomes cardiac) — one root, four languages, all still recognisable. The same root anchors Italian cuore, Portuguese coração, and Russian serdtse, each an independent inheritance of the identical PIE ancestor rather than a loan from any of the others.

Eastward, Bengali hridoy keeps हृदयम् (hṛdayam) whole, a तत्सम; its worn-down twin hiya survives only in poetry and song, not everyday speech — the rarer pairing, where the carried-whole word is the common one and the worn-down word is the rare one.

blocks.title: What you've built: twelve words, three rooms

segments.text: Three groups, twelve nouns: what you would ask for (pānīyam, kṣīram, annam), who you would introduce (mitram, kuṭumbam, bhrātā, bhaginī), and your own face (akṣi, karṇaḥ, mukham, nāsikā, hṛdayam). Almost every one of them ended in the neuter -म् you first named beside अन्नम् — and almost every one pointed at a word some other language in this project already teaches as its own.

segments.text: Name three languages, besides English, whose word for heart shares हृदयम् (hṛdayam)'s root. (Any three of Latin, Greek, Italian, Portuguese, Russian.) Which Bengali form of "heart" is everyday, and which survives only in poetry? (hridoy, everyday; hiya, poetry.) What gender has run through nearly this entire chapter's nouns? (Neuter.) And what was the very first word of this chapter? (Pānīyam, water.)
